campbell-popular-tales-west-highlands-18: J. F. Campbell's West Highland tale set ends with this fourth part, from the work of 1860. The tales were writ down in Gaelic by his team, word for word from the folk. Four parts in sum hold the great hoard of the Highlands. With this part, the store of seal folk, giants, and quest tales comes to its close. The notes and word lists round out the work of the whole vast set. It stands as the last word of the folk of the west Highlands in print.
coke-reports-1777-vol4:
Volume 4 of Wilson's 1777 edition of Coke's Reports gives more decisions from the courts Coke knew best. By the fourth volume, the set had become the working library of the English bar. Coke's name on a precedent carried weight that few judges before or since have matched.

Among the disputes here are clashes between the crown's claims and the subject's rights under the common law. Coke's wider fame rests on rulings of that kind, where he held that the king cannot change the law by proclamation alone. The reports show law used as a shield for freedom against prerogative power. Coke reports his own resistance with evident pride, and later lawyers, including the American founders, treated these pages as a storehouse of liberty.
degroot-religious-system-china-vol4:
Volume Four of de Groot's Religious System appeared in 1901 in English. Priesthoods take the center as he turns from beliefs to men. Taoist and Buddhist clergy, their orders, and their rites fill the book.

De Groot shows how the sacred callings were formed, ranked, and paid. Ordination, dress, temples, and daily tasks get patient, full treatment. He treats monks and priests as workers in a vast shared system. The human machinery of Chinese religion stands clear in this volume. His exhaustive manner suits the dense, practical subject very well indeed. Readers see faith as a trade, a rank, and a daily round.
dutt-agni-purana-vol4:
Volume 4 closes Dutt's Agni Puranam in his 1904 English rendering. Ritual, devotion, and the soul's release fill this final part. Four volumes complete the most wide-ranging of all the puranas.

Yoga, vows, and the worship of gods guide the book's last lessons. The path from daily duty to final freedom stands mapped in full. Agni's vast survey of Indian knowledge comes to its calm end. Readers who finish here hold a whole culture's store in view. Dutt's steady prose sees the great task through to its close at last. The set remains a bold feat of translation in its own right.
frazer-totemism-and-exogamy-1910-vol4:
The fourth and final volume of Frazer's 1910 treatise steps back from the mass of cases to theory. After three volumes of evidence on totem clans and marriage rules, Frazer asks what totemism finally is and how it relates to religion.

He reviews the main theories, including his own changing views, and weighs the idea that totemism grows from magic and early ideas of the soul. The volume closes with indexes and summary material for the whole work. Frazer's answers did not stand, but his questions set the agenda. Later fieldworkers defined their science partly by arguing with this book.
grimm-teutonic-mythology-1882-vol4: Jacob Grimm's Teutonic Mythology ends with this fourth part, in Stallybrass's English text of the 1888 print. The four parts in sum form the most vast book on German myth of its age. Grimm drew it from poems, laws, and lore across the whole north. The last part brings the long survey to its close and rounds out its themes. Gods, rites, charms, and the beings of wood and water all find their place in the scheme.
lamb-works-lucas-vol4:
Poems and plays fill the fourth volume of Lucas's 1903 Lamb edition. A frontispiece shows Charles Lamb at age twenty-three, drawn by Robert Hancock. The contents open with his earliest poem in Latin, then move through verses printed in Coleridge's books of 1796 and 1797.

Among the pieces are The Grandame, Childhood, The Sabbath Bells, and a sonnet to Cowper. Charles's blank-verse tragedy John Woodvil and the sad lyric The Old Familiar Faces also belong to this part of his output, by the v1 account. The Lambs were essayists first, yet these pages show real feeling in grander forms.
las-casas-historia-indias-vol4:
Volume 4 of the Historia, in the 1875 edition, reaches the core of the story. Las Casas takes up the conquest of Mexico in full detail. He also treats the great debate at Valladolid on Spain's rights there.

At Valladolid, Las Casas faced Sepúlveda in formal public debate before the court. One side claimed Spain could rule Native peoples by force of arms. The other held that faith must spread by peace and free choice. The fate of millions hung on fine points of law and faith. Spain's conscience speaks at full power in these famous pages.
middleton-works-dyce-1840-vol4:
Volume Four of Dyce's Middleton, from 1840, brings the collected plays toward their close. Middleton's later career included work for the King's Men and pageants for the City of London. Dyce prints the canon in the order the old editions allowed.

The plays here show the older dramatist's craft: tight plots, bold scenes, and a cold clarity about human appetite. His collaborations, a normal part of Jacobean stage life, appear beside his solo work. Games of chess and courts of law alike served his plots over the years. With one volume left, the set has rebuilt a major author from scattered quartos.
podcast-joerogan-6hrd9Z4gUL4:
Rogan argues, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, that the media keeps trying to debunk the Wuhan lab theory long after the ground shifted. The claim that COVID-19 may have escaped from a lab was once treated as fringe. Later it drew support from officials and scientists.

The segment follows the coverage itself: the firm early denials, the quiet corrections, and the writers who never revisited their calls. Rogan asks what the episode taught about trust in news during a crisis. It is a media-criticism hour from a host who believes the debunkers had motives beyond the facts.
podcast-joerogan-PC7etaZ2AL4:
Is the universe itself developing consciousness? Rogan asks that grand question in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The idea, found in some philosophy and fringe physics, holds that mind may be a basic feature of reality that grows as the cosmos grows.

The talk moves from the human brain outward, asking where awareness starts and whether it could scale to stars and systems. Rogan weighs the poetry of the idea against the lack of hard proof. The segment is pure late-night philosophy, the kind of open-ended wonder the show returns to when no guest is booked and the night is young.
podcast-tuckercarlson-5xnvaHlcaL4:
Former CIA officer Amaryllis Fox Kennedy joins Tucker Carlson to discuss Iraq, JFK, and everything else she says the intelligence agencies lie about. Fox Kennedy served undercover overseas before writing a memoir and marrying into the Kennedy family. Her confessional is candid about the spy life's costs.

She describes how the agency sold the Iraq war and what officers knew at the time. She gives her view of the Kennedy assassination files and the long secrecy around them. Carlson asks what reform could ever tame the agencies. Curious and brave viewers get a spy who saw too much, telling it plainly.
satow-tasj-vol4:
Volume Four of the Transactions, covering 1875 and 1876, appeared in 1876. Satow's circle of pioneer Japanologists reports another year of finds. Meiji Japan, new to outside study, fills their curious pages.

Papers range across history, folklore, language, and the natural world. Each adds one more block to the field's young foundations in Japan. The tone stays brisk, factual, and hungry for the next find. Readers watch a science form itself in real time, year by year. These modest volumes hold the seed of all later Japan studies in English. Their writers knew they were first, and they wrote like it.
